# ISO 27001 Certification — Tailored Plan

## Scope statement review

Your draft scope is solid. A few refinements to consider:

> "The Information Security Management System (ISMS) covering the development, delivery, and operation of [Company]'s SaaS platform hosted on Microsoft Azure, including supporting corporate IT systems, customer data processing activities, and third-party managed services, operated from [locations/remote]. Excluding: corporate marketing systems not connected to production data."

**Why the tweaks:**

- Auditors will probe **boundaries**. "Corporate marketing systems" needs to be defensible — if marketing tools touch customer PII or authenticate via the same SSO, they may get pulled in.
- **Third-party managed services** are in your supply chain and must be addressed (Annex A 5.19–5.22) even if partially outsourced.
- Specify **locations** (offices, remote work, Azure regions) because the certification is scoped to them.
- Mention **corporate IT** explicitly — auditors expect HR systems, endpoint management, and identity infrastructure to be in scope if employees use them to access production.

---

## Gap analysis checklist

Since you already hold SOC 2 Type II and run lightweight ITIL, you have a head start. The checklist below focuses on **what SOC 2 typically leaves uncovered** or underdocumented for ISO 27001.

# ISO 27001 Certification — Continued

---

## Phase 2 — Build and implement (Months 4–6)

**Month 4 — Supplier security, asset classification, and SDLC**

- Conduct supplier risk assessments for top-tier vendors (Azure, managed service providers, critical SaaS tools)
- Insert ISO 27001 clauses into vendor contracts and DPAs where missing
- Define and publish data classification scheme (e.g., Public / Internal / Confidential / Restricted)
- Assign asset and data owners across business units
- Formalize secure development lifecycle:
  - Security requirements in user stories
  - Threat modelling for major features
  - SAST/DAST integration in CI/CD
  - Security sign-off gate before production release
- Document secure coding standards

> 🏁 **Milestone: Supplier register assessed, classification scheme live, SDLC policy approved**

**Month 5 — BCP/DR, legal register, operational controls**

- Build or update Business Continuity Plan and IT Disaster Recovery Plan
- Define RTO and RPO per critical service
- Run a tabletop exercise and an Azure region failover test; document results
- Create register of applicable legislation, regulations, and contractual obligations
- Review and document:
  - Remote working policy (6.7)
  - Information deletion and retention schedule (8.10)
  - Data masking in non-production environments (8.11)
  - DLP controls or documented risk acceptance (8.12)
  - Threat intelligence sources and consumption process (5.7)
- Review cryptographic controls and key management documentation (8.24)
- Verify clock synchronization, log retention, and audit log integrity (8.17, 8.15, 8.34)

> 🏁 **Milestone: BCP/DR tested with evidence, legal register complete, operational control gaps closed**

**Month 6 — People controls, awareness, and measurement**

- Deliver second awareness training module with a measured assessment (quiz, phishing simulation, completion tracking)
- Review HR processes:
  - Background screening covers contractors (6.1)
  - Employment contracts include security responsibilities (6.2)
  - Disciplinary process references security violations (6.4)
  - Offboarding checklist verified with access revocation SLA (6.5)
- Define ISMS KPIs and begin measurement (9.1):
  - Percentage of risks treated on schedule
  - Mean time to revoke leaver access
  - Vulnerability patching SLA compliance
  - Awareness training completion rate
  - Incident response time vs target
- Collect first month of KPI data
- Review and finalize all remaining SoA control evidence

> 🏁 **Milestone: All 93 Annex A controls implemented or formally risk-accepted, KPI baseline established**

---

## Phase 3 — Assure and certify (Months 7–9)

**Month 7 — Internal audit**

- Execute full internal audit covering:
  - All ISMS clauses (4–10)
  - All applicable Annex A controls from the SoA
- Use independent auditors (internal staff not responsible for the area, or outsource to a consultancy — do **not** use your certification body for this to avoid conflict of interest)
- Classify findings:
  - **Major nonconformity**: requirement not met or entire process absent
  - **Minor nonconformity**: isolated lapse, evidence gap
  - **Opportunity for improvement**: working but could be stronger
- Issue internal audit report with findings and corrective action requests
- Assign corrective action owners and due dates (all must close before Stage 2)

> 🏁 **Milestone: Internal audit report issued, corrective action plan in progress**

**Month 8 — Management review and Stage 1 audit**

- Close all corrective actions from internal audit with evidence of effectiveness
- Hold formal management review meeting with minutes covering the mandatory agenda (9.3.2):
  - Status of actions from previous reviews
  - Changes in external/internal issues
  - Nonconformities and corrective actions
  - Monitoring and measurement results (KPIs)
  - Audit results
  - Risk assessment and treatment status
  - Opportunities for continual improvement
  - Resource needs
- Executive signs off on management review minutes and decisions
- **Stage 1 audit** (documentation review, typically 1–2 days on-site or remote):
  - Certification body reviews ISMS documentation, scope, SoA, risk assessment, policies
  - Outcome: readiness opinion and any areas of concern for Stage 2
  - You receive a list of issues to address before Stage 2
- Fix any Stage 1 findings immediately

> 🏁 **Milestone: Management review complete, Stage 1 passed with no blocking issues**

**Month 9 — Stage 2 audit and certification**

- Final evidence review: ensure every SoA control has accessible, current evidence
- Brief all control owners on what to expect (auditor interviews, evidence walkthroughs)
- **Stage 2 audit** (certification audit, typically 4–6 days for a 250-person org):
  - Auditors sample controls, interview staff, review evidence
  - They assess implementation effectiveness, not just documentation
  - Findings classified as major nonconformity, minor nonconformity, or OFI
- **If major nonconformities**: certification withheld until resolved (usually a follow-up audit within 90 days)
- **If only minor nonconformities**: certificate issued; you submit a corrective action plan within an agreed timeframe (typically 90 days) and evidence is reviewed at the next surveillance audit
- **If clean or OFI only**: certificate issued

> 🏁 **Milestone: ISO 27001 certificate issued 🎉**

**Post-certification (ongoing)**

- Surveillance audits at 6 or 12-month intervals (certification body decides)
- Continue internal audit cycle annually
- Hold management reviews at least annually (most orgs do quarterly)
- Recertification audit in year 3
- Continual improvement: treat the ISMS as a living system, not a project

## Estimated auditor days for certification

ISO 27001 audit duration is calculated based on **IAF Mandatory Document 26** (MD 26), which uses the number of effective personnel in scope. For 250 employees in a mid-complexity SaaS organization:

### Stage 1 (documentation review)

| Item | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Auditor days | **2–3 days** |
| Format | On-site or remote (certification body preference) |
| Auditors | 1 lead auditor (possibly 1 technical expert for cloud/SaaS) |
| Purpose | Review ISMS documentation, scope, SoA, risk assessment; confirm readiness for Stage 2 |
| Typical output | Readiness report with observations and areas of concern |
| Gap between Stage 1 and Stage 2 | Minimum 2 weeks, recommended 4–6 weeks to address findings |

### Stage 2 (certification audit)

| Item | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Auditor days | **7–10 days** |
| Format | Primarily on-site with some remote evidence review possible |
| Auditors | 1 lead auditor + 1 auditor (possibly 1 technical expert) |
| Duration | Typically 4–5 calendar days with 2 auditors working in parallel |
| Purpose | Assess implementation effectiveness of the ISMS and all SoA controls |
| Activities | Staff interviews (8–15 people), evidence sampling, process walkthroughs, observation |
| Typical output | Audit report with findings (major NC, minor NC, OFI), recommendation for certification |

### How MD 26 calculates it

| Effective personnel in scope | Audit duration (Stage 1 + Stage 2 combined) |
|---|---|
| 126–175 | 10–12 auditor days |
| 176–275 | 11–14 auditor days |
| 276–425 | 12–15 auditor days |

For 250 people, you land in the **11–14 day range** total. The split is roughly 25% Stage 1 and 75% Stage 2, giving you approximately 3 + 9 = 12 days as a midpoint estimate. Certification bodies may adjust slightly based on:

- **Reductions** (up to 30%): mature SOC 2, low complexity, single site, single Azure region, well-documented processes
- **Increases**: multiple locations, highly regulated data (health, finance), complex supply chain, multiple development teams

> **Your org's profile** (SOC 2 in place, single product, mostly cloud, lightweight ITIL) likely qualifies for a modest reduction. Budget for **3 Stage 1 days + 8 Stage 2 days = 11 total auditor days** as a planning estimate.

## Step 1 — Likelihood scale

| Score | Label | Description | Approximate frequency |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rare | Could occur only in exceptional circumstances | Less than once in 5 years |
| 2 | Unlikely | Could occur but not expected | Once in 2–5 years |
| 3 | Possible | Might occur at some point | Once per year |
| 4 | Likely | Will probably occur in most circumstances | Multiple times per year |
| 5 | Almost certain | Expected to occur frequently or already occurring | Monthly or more often |

## Step 2 — Impact scale

| Score | Label | Confidentiality | Integrity | Availability | Financial | Regulatory / legal | Reputational |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Negligible | Exposure of public data only | Error detected and corrected immediately | <15 min downtime | <$10k loss | No regulatory interest | No external awareness |
| 2 | Minor | Internal data exposed to small group | Minor data error, limited scope | 15 min–2 hr downtime | $10k–$50k | Regulatory inquiry possible | Limited customer awareness |
| 3 | Moderate | Confidential data exposed internally | Data corruption requiring restore from backup | 2–8 hr downtime | $50k–$250k | Regulatory investigation | Industry media coverage |
| 4 | Major | Customer PII exposed externally | Significant data loss, partial unrecoverable | 8–24 hr downtime | $250k–$1M | Formal regulatory action / fine | National media coverage |
| 5 | Severe | Mass customer data breach | Widespread data destruction | >24 hr downtime | >$1M | Licence / certification revoked | Lasting brand damage, customer loss |

**Rule:** When a risk affects multiple impact categories, use the **highest** single-category score.
